title: Battle of Kumsong (1953): The Last Offensive of the Korean War
subtitle: July 13 – July 27, 1953

lines: The night of July 13th, 1953. A mountain front south of Kumsong, in central Korea.
As darkness fell, the entire ridgeline to the north erupted in fire.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Before the guns even slackened, Chinese troops came pouring down every valley.
By midnight, in some places, they were already a thousand meters inside the South Korean lines.
scenes.label: Dramatization

callouts.text: US Army history: up to 1,000 m by midnight

lines: The armistice would be signed in just fourteen days.
And with two weeks left, the last great offensive of the Korean War had begun.
The Battle of Kumsong.
This is the story of the war's final battle, fought over the last stretch of today's armistice line.
By June 1953, the truce talks at Panmunjom were nearly done.
After two years of deadlock over prisoners, both sides finally agreed.
On June 8th, the prisoner exchange deal was signed. Peace seemed days away.

callouts.text: JUNE 1953 · FINAL STAGE OF TRUCE TALKS

lines: But South Korean President Syngman Rhee bitterly opposed any truce that left Korea divided.
On June 18th, he suddenly set free some twenty-seven thousand anti-communist prisoners who had refused repatriation.
The communists were furious.
And before signing any truce, they resolved to teach the South Korean army a hard lesson.
General Mark Clark believed a main aim was to give the ROK Army a bloody nose.
scenes.label: Anti-communist ex-POWs arriving in Seoul after release (1953)

lines: They chose a bulge in the central front, pushing north toward the town of Kumsong.
It was called the Kumsong salient.
It was held by the ROK Capital Division and the divisions of ROK II Corps.
Open to the enemy on three sides, it favored the attacker.
ROK II Corps was commanded by Lieutenant General Chung Il-kwon.
His corps had already been pushed back once in June, and a far bigger storm was gathering.
To the north, five Chinese armies, some two hundred forty thousand men, were massing.
Behind them stood about thirteen hundred sixty guns.
After the prisoner release, Mao reportedly ordered a heavier blow.
In men and in firepower, this time the enemy held the advantage.
It was a final gamble to draw the line even one meter farther south before the truce.
On July 13th, as the sun went down, the communist guns opened fire all at once.
In moments, the South Korean positions were engulfed in flames.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: From July 11th, in ten days, the communists fired about one hundred ninety-seven thousand shells.
It was the heaviest ten-day bombardment of the war.

visual.sub: Communist artillery, July 11–20, 1953 · 10-day record of the war (US Army history)

lines: Then the Chinese drove like wedges into both shoulders of the salient.
The Capital Division in the west and the ROK 3rd Division in the east broke in turn.
In the dark, the enemy slipped behind the lines and struck command posts.
Colonel Yuk Geun-su of the Capital Division was killed trying to rescue his surrounded 1st Regiment.
scenes.label: Dramatization

callouts.text: NIGHT OF JULY 14 · COL. YUK GEUN-SU KILLED

lines: In the center, four enemy battalions surrounded a battalion of the ROK 6th Division.
Phone lines were cut. No one knew which positions still held.
scenes.label: Dramatization

callouts.text: US Army history · ROK 19th Regiment front

lines: On July 14th, Eighth Army commander General Maxwell Taylor made a hard decision.
Give up the salient, fall back south of the Kumsong River, and rebuild the line.

callouts.text: JULY 14, 1953 · WITHDRAW SOUTH OF KUMSONG RIVER

lines: But in the rain and confusion, the withdrawal began to fall apart.
Some units retreated across the river and far beyond the line they had been ordered to hold.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The enemy's next objective lay south: the Hwachon Reservoir.
If it fell, even the Hwachon power plant that sent electricity to Seoul would be in danger.
Behind the broken front, the South Koreans stitched together a new line along the high ridges.
It ran from Chokkun-san in the west, through Chupa Pass, to Paegam-san in the east.

callouts.text: NEW LINE · CHOKKUN-SAN – CHUPA PASS – PAEGAM-SAN (APPROX.)

lines: Chokkun-san rises one thousand seventy-three meters. Paegam-san, one thousand one hundred seventy-nine.
Lose these peaks, and there were no high mountains left between the enemy and Hwachon.
General Chung brought up the reserve 11th Division and pulled the battered 6th and 3rd back to regroup.
In the west, the US 3rd Division and the airlifted 187th Airborne rushed in.

callouts.text: JULY 14–15 · ROK 11TH DIV COMMITTED · US 3RD DIV & 187TH ABN

lines: Meanwhile, torrential rain forced the Chinese to halt and catch their breath.
It gave the South Koreans one chance to strike back.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: On July 16th, ROK II Corps counterattacked with the 11th, 8th, and 5th Divisions abreast.
Their objective was simple: retake the high ground south of the Kumsong River.
Climbing slopes slick with mud, the soldiers took back the hills one by one.
Night after night, the enemy struck back hard to keep what it had won.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Among the fiercest fights was Paegam-san, lost to the Chinese.
With the 5th Division stopped, the attached 7th Regiment swung in from the north and retook the summit.
Around Paegam-san alone, some five hundred seventy South Koreans were killed or missing.
On July 19th, the South Koreans finally stood on the high ground south of the Kumsong River.
But efforts to retake the old positions across the river had to be abandoned after the 20th.

callouts.text: JULY 19, 1953 · RIDGELINE SOUTH OF THE RIVER SECURED

lines: For the final week of the war, ROK II Corps held this Kumsong River line.
And on July 27th, the armistice was signed at Panmunjom.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: At ten o'clock that night, the guns at last fell silent.
The armistice line was drawn along the very ground where the two sides stood at that moment.
scenes.label: Gen. Mark W. Clark signs the armistice (July 27, 1953)

lines: The ridgeline south of the Kumsong River, retaken in blood, became this stretch of today's armistice line.
Had it lain just a few kilometers farther south, the map of Hwachon might look very different today.

callouts.text: SOUTH OF KUMSONG RIVER ≈ TODAY'S DEMARCATION LINE (APPROX.)

lines: The salient itself was lost, about one hundred seventy square kilometers.
By South Korean counts, some fourteen thousand ROK soldiers were killed, wounded, or missing. Eighth Army estimated over twenty-eight thousand Chinese casualties.

visual.note: ROK: South Korean counts (sources vary) · Chinese: Eighth Army estimate

lines: So why could two hundred forty thousand troops never break through to Hwachon?
Let's look at four reasons.
First, the salient trap.
Touching the enemy on three sides, the salient's shoulders were its weak points from the start.
Once a shoulder broke, every unit inside was at risk of being surrounded.
Second, the mountain defense line.
The South Koreans did not fall back to open ground, but redrew their line on peaks over a thousand meters high.
Holding the heights, they could stand firm with far fewer men.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Third, reserves and reinforcements.
The corps pulled out its shattered divisions and threw the reserve 11th Division straight in.
With American reinforcements arriving within a day or two, the gap never widened.
Fourth, the counterattack in the rain.
The South Koreans did not waste the days when the enemy paused for breath.
When the side being pushed back struck first, the enemy's final breakthrough lost its momentum.
After July 20th, the Chinese advanced no farther south.
scenes.label: A wounded Chinese sniper treated and questioned after capture (July 16, 1953)

lines: About a decade after the war, a young officer was serving as a platoon leader near Paegam-san.
In those mountains, he came across nameless graves marked by nothing but a wooden stake.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: That officer, Han Myung-hee, wrote the Korean art song Bimok, The Wooden Marker.
The deep valley in that song was these very mountains.

visual.sub: Lyrics by Han Myung-hee · inspired by nameless graves near Paegam-san

lines: In autumn 2025, remains were recovered from a nameless hill in Cheorwon.
They were Sergeant Kim Sun-sik of the ROK 6th Division, killed at Kumsong eight days before the truce.
This May, after seventy-three years, he finally came home to his family.
The line south of the Kumsong River is still drawn over the names of men like him.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Fourteen days before the truce, a final offensive by two hundred forty thousand men.
The line that refused to break before it is today's armistice line.

items.text: The great offensive, 14 days before the truce
The last line, held with blood
